Many recent formalizations of Erdos problems have ended up being conditional on one of the following versions of the Mertens theorems:

  1. (First theorem) ∑p≤xlog⁡pp=log⁡x+O(1)\sum_{p \leq x} \frac{\log p}{p} = \log x + O(1)∑p≤x​plogp​=logx+O(1); ∑n≤xΛ(n)n=log⁡x+O(1)\sum_{n \leq x} \frac{\Lambda(n)}{n} = \log x + O(1)∑n≤x​nΛ(n)​=logx+O(1)
  2. (Second theorem) ∑p≤x1p=log⁡log⁡x+M+O(1log⁡x)\sum_{p \leq x} \frac{1}{p} = \log\log x + M + O(\frac{1}{\log x})∑p≤x​p1​=loglogx+M+O(logx1​); ∑n≤xΛ(n)nlog⁡n=log⁡log⁡x+γ+O(1log⁡x)\sum_{n \leq x} \frac{\Lambda(n)}{n\log n} = \log\log x + \gamma + O(\frac{1}{\log x})∑n≤x​nlognΛ(n)​=loglogx+γ+O(logx1​), where M,γM, \gammaM,γ are the Meissel-Mertens and Euler-Mascheroni constants respectively
  3. (Third theorem) ∏p≤x(1−1p)=1+O(1log⁡x)eγlog⁡x.\prod_{p \leq x} (1-\frac{1}{p}) = \frac{1 + O(\frac{1}{\log x})}{e^\gamma \log x}.∏p≤x​(1−p1​)=eγlogx1+O(logx1​)​.

These theorems can probably be extracted from what is already in the PNT+ project, but this requires a lot of dependencies and is also not written in a streamlined style. So I was thinking it would be worthwhile to try to create a Mathlib suitable proof of these theorems (perhaps with non-optimal constants in order to make the proofs more streamlined). But I have not actually tried to upstream anything to Mathlib before and am asking for advice on how to proceed. I took the liberty of creating an initial blueprint for the first two theorems here, following some notes of Leo Goldmakher, with initial stubs here.

I am sure that all the sorries here could be readily filled in by modern autoformalization tools; however, such a formalization may not be suitable for Mathlib upstreaming, and so I am not currently assigning these sorries as tasks in the PNT project. Instead, I'd like to hear from anyone with experience on Mathlib upstreaming for advice on how to structure the proofs here to make it easier to upstream later, and whether one should add more "API" around these results as well.

Hi Terry, we've also been trying to upstream the Iwaniec-Kowalski project as we go (which is partly why it's going so slowly; we're up to equation (1.35)...), please see, e.g., here. I think your Mertens targets are fine; there's not really a more "general" way to sum log⁡n\log nlogn up to xxx (is there?), so I don't think they'll want more generality than that. What we sometimes do in I-K is let an AI fill in a proof, and then spend some time golfing it. You also might want more API; e.g., explicit constants like E₁p x ≤ log 4 + 4 are nice but you could add E₁p = O[atTop] 1, in case a later user just needs the asymptotic version, etc. We've found it useful to discuss such decisions over in-person meetings / zoom calls...

You might be interested in this unfinished project of mine, all human-written, which proves the following forms of Mertens' theorems in ~1000 LoC following the proof in Tenenbaum. These are all conditional on the result that ψ(x)≪x.\psi(x) \ll x.ψ(x)≪x.

theorem mertens_first : (fun n : ℕ ↦ (∑ p ∈ primesBelow (n+1), Real.log p / p) - Real.log n)
    =O[⊤] (fun _ ↦ (1 : ℝ))

theorem mertens_second (a : ℝ) (ha : 1 < a) (ha' : a < 2)
: (fun t : ℝ ↦ (∑ p ∈ primesBelow (⌊t⌋₊+1), (p : ℝ)⁻¹) - (Real.log (Real.log t) + mertens₂Const))
    =O[𝓟 (Set.Ioi a)] (fun n ↦ (Real.log n)⁻¹)

theorem mertens_third :
    IsEquivalent atTop (fun x ↦ ∏ p ∈ primesBelow (⌊x⌋₊ + 1), (1 - (p : ℝ)⁻¹))
      (fun x ↦ exp (- mertens₃Const) * (Real.log x)⁻¹)

The main thing missing is the fact that the constant in Mertens' third theorem is γ\gammaγ. Also third theorem here uses o(1)o(1)o(1) instead of O(1/log⁡x)O(1/\log x)O(1/logx), but I do also have a log-version with a O(1/log⁡x)O(1/\log x)O(1/logx) bound so it shouldn't be too difficult to derive the version you stated.

The code itself isn't particularly nice. There are some very long proofs that should be broken up, and a number of the intermediate lemmas that aren't up to Mathlib's standards. I had intended to upstream these to Mathlib at some point (after computing the constant in the third theorem), but I've been distracted working on other things. And frankly I'd figured we would be able to derive them from the PNT, but I guess upstreaming that is taking longer than I'd expected.

It might still make sense to write the proof in this blueprint if the goal is to focus on writing Mathlib-quality code from the start. I do think there are some results in my file that might be of interest about log⁡(n!)\log (n!)log(n!).

Thanks! I will update the file to add more API and a link to Arend's repository. I think many of the lemmas there can also be added as additional API if they are not redundant. And any humans trying to prove the lemmas in the blueprint may well be able to use this partial codebase as inspiration.

The bound ψ(x)≪x\psi(x) \ll xψ(x)≪x is now in Mathlib (with a constant of 4+log⁡24+\log 24+log2), see docs#Chebyshev.psi_le_const_mul_self. We have sharper bounds in Chebyshev.lean but these have a lot of dependencies (including LeanCert) and so would not be suitable for upstreaming.

I've also added more arguments computing the constant in Mertens third theorem. Once the latest PR merges, I will start creating tasks for humans to try to fill in the sorries with as efficient and structured code as possible (in particular, I will strongly discourage AI-generated solutions for these tasks).

OK, I have launched some initial tasks PNT#1303 - PNT#1309 to claim regarding Mertens' first theorem. Again, I stress here that this is intended to be Mathlib quality, and so should be mostly written by hand with minimal AI assistance, with an eye towards having efficient, well-structured proofs. For some reason the issues are not all showing up properly on Github, but hopefully this is a temporary glitch. I'll add further tasks shortly.

I have a repository generated by Aristotle that gives the exponential form, namely LCM(1...n) < 4^n. See #PrimeNumberTheorem+ > Bounds on LCM(1..n) in Mathlib for a mathematical summary. The repository has <500loc which include other results for a project I am working on. Aristotle followed my blueprint nicely. Would anyone here be interested in adapting the result? For the Chebyshev bound the exponential form in repository could probably be extracted and reduced to <300 loc simply by cutting out the parts that aren't needed for the Chebyshev bound.

content: I've now assigned tasks PNT#1303 - PNT#1330 for all the outstanding sorries in the Mertens file. Feel free to claim any of these to work on, bearing in mind that these proofs are intended to be upstreamed to Mathlib and so require significant human attention. Some of the code from Arend's repository (or other parts of PNT+, such as Chebyshev.lean) may be useful as inspiration, but do try to keep the code in Mertens.lean self-contained (using only Mathlib imports) and as high quality as possible.

Hi Terry, one little comment: in my experience with Mathlib, the maintainers care not only about the proofs being tight, but the statements as well. They’ll ask whether the statements are the most abstract possible, whether they should be refactored to follow from more general statements, where in the library they likely belong, etc. For example, if something has been proved nicely but should really follow from Stieljes integration, they may well ask for the latter to be formalized as a prerequisite... (Though maybe they'll be more lenient with you?...) Also, I’m not sure that I would necessarily discourage AI use in formalization, but just ask for a higher level of proof quality (which can, with work, be obtained with AI help…).

Thanks for the comments! Indeed Stieltjes integration may be a pain point. In the applications here, the weights are continuously differentiable (they are things like t↦1/log⁡tt \mapsto 1/\log tt↦1/logt), or at least piecewise continuously differentiable (think of t↦⌊t⌋t \mapsto \lfloor t \rfloort↦⌊t⌋ for instance) and one can replace all Stieltjes integration steps with the fundamental theorem of calculus and Fubini's theorem instead, both of which are already in Mathlib. I'm thinking that the world of ContDiff weights is already pretty rich and has plenty of API support in Mathlib, so I may end up just developing some summation-by-parts machinery in this setting without trying to set up all of Riemann-Stieltjes integration in Mathlib, which seems worthwhile but is something of a mission creep for this Mertens project.

By the way, we do already have in PNT+ theorems like sum_eq_int_deriv, so in this case, it could be a matter of cleaning up existing proof code, which may be slightly easier (?) than coming up with the code in the first place... (This is for, e.g., Mertens-sum-log)

Yes, I am hoping that many results already PNT+ (or in @Arend Mellendijk 's repository, etc.) can be repurposed, with the main task indeed being the "cleaning" and removing of unnecessary dependencies. @Alastair Irving has just made a similar point on the issue page.

Looking at PNT#1316, the upper bound for E1E_1E1​, I wonder if we really want an explicit upper bound here or just to show that the sum is convergent. We could then just have subsequent results depending on the constant E1E_1E1​. Mathlib seems to be lacking a nice version of the integral test (see the todos in SumIntegralComparisons.lean). An alternative would be to crudely estimate log⁡n\log nlogn by n\sqrt nn​ and then use the summability of n−3/2n^{-3/2}n−3/2 which would also give an upper bound in terms of ζ(3/2)\zeta(3/2)ζ(3/2).

Good point. I've submitted PNT#1351 to add a separate lemma establishing summability for E1E_1E1​. For the purposes of getting a completely explicit bound it is still worth getting some control on E1E_1E1​ within Mathlib (and we could keep some more accurate bounds, using e.g., LeanCert, here in the PNT+ repository), but I agree that for many applications just knowing that E1E_1E1​ exists as a well-defined constant given by an absolutely convergent series is enough.

There will be a similar issue later on when I define an internal version of the Euler-Mascheroni constant as an expression involving an integral of an error E1,ΛE_{1,\Lambda}E1,Λ​, as one will need a separate theorem that that integrand is absolutely integrable; I will look at that later today. EDIT: never mind, the repository already has private theorem integrable_E₁Λ_div_mul_log_sq (although the proof is sorried right now).
Thank you, I'm using your new summability result in my proof of PNT#1312

Thinking about the formula for log⁡ζ\log\zetalogζ in PNT#1319. I wonder if the initial reduction
log⁡ζ(s)=∑nΛ(n)nslog⁡n \log \zeta(s) = \sum_n \frac{\Lambda(n)}{n^s \log n}logζ(s)=∑n​nslognΛ(n)​
should be separated into its own task unles that already exists in Mathlib. I'm not sure of the best way to prove it. We can take logs in the Euler product and taylor expand but rearranging the double sum doesn't sound fun. Alternatively can we use the existing expansion of ζ′/ζ=∑Λ\zeta'/\zeta=\sum \Lambdaζ′/ζ=∑Λ in a clever way? The required identity differentiates to this so we should be able to use the identity theorem although we'd need to get the constant correct somehow.

Good questions. I think using the log derivative is the best way forward. First one shows that
ddslog⁡ζ(s)=ζ′ζ(s) \frac{d}{ds} \log \zeta(s) = \frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(s)dsd​logζ(s)=ζζ′​(s)
for s>1s>1s>1, and then by using the asymptotic ζ(s)→1\zeta(s) \to 1ζ(s)→1 as s→+∞s \to +\inftys→+∞ deduces that
log⁡ζ(s)=∫s∞−ζ′ζ(u) du. \log \zeta(s) = \int_s^\infty -\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(u)\ du.logζ(s)=∫s∞​−ζζ′​(u) du.
Then substitute −ζ′ζ(u)=∑n=1∞Λ(n)nu-\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(u) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{\Lambda(n)}{n^u}−ζζ′​(u)=∑n=1∞​nuΛ(n)​ and integrate term by term using Tonelli's theorem.
There is docs#ArithmeticFunction.LSeries_vonMangoldt_eq_deriv_riemannZeta_div in Mathlib, which does the first step.

We are now really close to finishing the Mertens theorem subproject - special thanks to @Alastair Irving for the most recent push! There are two sorries remaining: one being to use the second Mertens theorem to establish an asymptotic for log⁡ζ(s)=∑nΛ(n)/nslog⁡n\log \zeta(s) = \sum_n \Lambda(n) / n^s \log nlogζ(s)=∑n​Λ(n)/nslogn as −log⁡(s−1)+Γ′(1)+γ-\log(s-1) + \Gamma'(1) + \gamma−log(s−1)+Γ′(1)+γ plus a lower order term (PNT#1319), and the other to use this asymptotic, and the known asymptotic for zeta log⁡ζ(s)=−log⁡(s−1)+o(1)\log \zeta(s) = -\log(s-1) + o(1)logζ(s)=−log(s−1)+o(1), to conclude that our custom definition of the Euler Mascheroni constant γ\gammaγ agrees with the Mathlib one (which is known to be −Γ′(1)-\Gamma'(1)−Γ′(1)) PNT#1320. After that I think I can initiate the process of upstreaming the Mertens theorems to Mathlib!

P.S. I agree that we should establish log⁡ζ(s)=∑nΛ(n)nslog⁡n\log \zeta(s) = \sum_n \frac{\Lambda(n)}{n^s \log n}logζ(s)=∑n​nslognΛ(n)​ as a standalone theorem, ideally for the complex case Res>1\mathrm{Re} s > 1Res>1 and not just the real case s>1s > 1s>1 as that is also worth having.

I am now upstreaming the First Mertens theorem to Mathilb at #40656. If all goes well, I then plan to upstream the second. The Third is nearly done; the only issues are the aforementioned PNT#1319 and PNT#1320.

UPDATE: the previous contributor claiming PNT#1319 and PNT#1320 has disclaimed the tasks due to lack of time. If someone else wishes to take it on, feel free (but bear in mind that this is for Mathlib, so an overly large, AI-generated proof is not preferred).

I think these remainig tasks are quite hard and might benefit from being broken down further. Perhaps you could pull out the proof of
log⁡ζ(s)=∑nΛ(n)nslog⁡n\log \zeta(s) = \sum_n \frac{\Lambda(n)}{n^s \log n}logζ(s)=∑n​nslognΛ(n)​
into its own task. I might claim some of this eventually but am very happy if someone else jumps in first.
Good suggestion. I've done such a splitting at PNT#1575, will issue tasks once it all builds properly.
OK, PNT#1582-#1586 splits off five subtasks from the original PNT#1319 and PNT#1320, which remain but should be significantly simpler.

Some updates on the Mertens subproject. Firstly, we have all sorries filled! Thanks to everyone who contributed.

But the project is not done; many of the contributed proofs are quite lengthy (particularly the AI-generated ones) and will need to be golfed substantially. I am going to try to do this mostly by hand, focusing on the second Mertens theorem material; I will use this branch to record progress. My first plan is to refactor the arguments that convert bounds on E₁Λ to bounds on E₂Λ, and bounds on E₁p to bounds on E₂p, into a single abstract theorem that can be applied to both. The more challenging thing is to figure out how to simplify the proof that our artificially defined Euler-Mascheroni constant matches the Mathlib one, which is currently is about 350 lines, though it does contain some independently useful facts such as the Dirichlet series for the log of zeta. But I will deal with that later.

Meanwhile, the first Mertens theorem continues to exist as a pull request to Mathlib at #40656; I structured it to be dependent on three minor PRs, of which one is already merged. It turns out that Yuan Yi had independently also submitted a PR for Mertens' first theorem, which only bounds what we would call |E₁p N| for N: Nat, but obtained a superior bound of 2 (compared to our log 4 + 4), mainly thanks to an improved bound for E₁ = 0.755366...; we had obtained a bound of (5 * log 2 + 3) / 4 = 1.6164..., but Yuan obtained the sharper bound of 1 by a similar method. I managed to merge in Yuan's improvements while still golfing the file; the current PR'ed version of Mertens.lean sits at 420 lines, compared to 490 lines for Yuan's code and 911 lines for the IEANTN version, although the latter comparison is somewhat unfair as this version also contains blueprint metadata, as well as some Euler-Maclaurin estimates that I omitted in the Mathlib PR. In any case it illustrates that the process of converting formalized proofs to Mathlib-quality proofs is non-trivial!

More updates on the Mertens project. The aforementioned refactor is now complete, and the revised Mathlib PR at #40656 now contains an abstract concept of a "Mertens weight" which is basically an arithmetic function that enjoys the lower and upper bounds needed for Mertens first theorem, and Mertens second theorem for such functions is derived as a corollary of this after Abel summation. One then constructs two instances of this weight - a "von Mangoldt weight" Mertens.Weight.vonMangoldt and "prime weight" Mertens.Weight.prime - at which point all the classical first and second Mertens theorems become two-line corollaries. The PR now consists of 970 lines of code plus several helper lemmas in other files (which are separate pending PRs), compared to 1162 lines in the original file; so the golfing is less dramatic, but I think the infrastructure is more sound, for instance it will be easier in the future to establish Mertens type theorems in number fields or in arithmetic progressions with this formalism. (Also there are now many more versions of the first and second theorems in the PR than there were initially, including versions specialized to natural number inputs.)

Beyond this PR, the remaining tasks are to upstream the proofs that the constant in the von Mangoldt Mertens second theorem (now called Mertens.Weight.vonMangoldt.M) is equal to eulerMascheroni, and then establish the third Mertens theorem. A first step in this direction was to upstream the proof of the Dirichlet series formula for log zeta (to the right of the critical strip); this is now submitted at #41097, where I also generalized it to logarithms of Dirichlet L-functions.

I think the next target for upstreaming is the identity  (s - 1) * ∫ x in .Ioi 1, log (log x) * x^(-s) = - log (s - 1) + deriv Gamma 1 which should fit somewhere in the Gamma function portion of Mathlib. We have a largely AI-generated proof of this, but it should be feasible with some effort to convert it to a Mathlib-suitable submission.

#41120 is now submitted to obtain various identities for either deriv Gamma 1 or eulerMascheroni, in particular the identity (s - 1) * ∫ x in .Ioi 1, log (log x) * x^(-s) = - log (s - 1) - eulerMascheroni is established.

The planned next step is to upstream various asymptotics involving the zeta function near s = 1, specifically targeting log (riemannZeta s) = - log (s - 1) + o(1), which would be of independent interest.

After that, the next natural step would be to augment the theory of Mertens weights. Right now, #40656 shows that if ∑ n ∈ Ioc 0 ⌊ x ⌋₊, f n = log x + O(1) then ∑ n ∈ Ioc 0 ⌊ x ⌋₊, f n / log n = log (log x) + M + o(1) for a certain explicit constant M. Standard calculations (for which we essentially already have a lengthy AI-generated formalization for), including the identity mentioned above, also show that ∑ n ∈ Ioc 0 ⌊ x ⌋₊, f n / (n^(s-1) * log n) = - log (s - 1) + M - eulerMascheroni + o(1). Combining this with the asymptotics for zeta and the identity at #41097, this shows that M = eulerMascheroni.

Another Mathlib PR at #41205 that upstreams the required asymptotics for log zeta near s=1. The way I decided to structure it was to first show that zeta can be written as the product of 1/s-1 and an entire function, take logarithms, and use continuity properties of the log of the entire function. The same technique also gives some related asymptotics for the derivative, log-derivative, and inverse of zeta near s=1, which I have also added.

The full suite of Mertens theorems is now PR'ed at #41394 (superseding the previous PR at #40656). It is 1400 lines of code plus an additional 600 lines spread out over six auxiliary PRs, so it will take a while to get reviewed and merged (this is not counting a couple previous precursor PRs that are already merged). The process of converting bespoke PNT code (originally 2500 lines or so) to reusable Mathlib code was significantly more time-consuming than I expected, but I learned quite a bit about Mathlib code standards in the process.
